p: Monday, November 23, eleven at night, the station kitchen, a quiet hour on a twenty four. Jordan had Abby's text open on her phone and the regulations open on the station laptop, which was against some policy nobody had ever explained to her. Three hours of night. Ten full stops. One cross-country of over a hundred nautical miles, total distance.
Her mother's text had come in at 6:15 and she'd been carrying it around all shift like a stone in a shoe.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Sunday the 13th. Velarde's at 6:30. Same as always. Claire is driving me and the baby. You come too.

Velarde's was in Pueblo. It had been in Pueblo since before her mother was born there, a long room with red vinyl booths and a back room that the family took over on the Saturday nearest December 13 most years, and on December 13 itself when it fell on a weekend, whether or not the restaurant had planned on it. Her mother would be sixty three. It would be the first birthday without Danny.

And Danny had flown to it. Every year since he got his certificate, he'd flown Biscuit or a rental down to Pueblo Memorial, and somebody's cousin had picked him up in a truck, and Lourdes had sat in the back room with her phone face up on the table next to her plate until it buzzed. Jordan had driven. Every year. She'd been the one who brought the cake in the trunk.

She pulled up the chart on the laptop and measured it with the cursor because she didn't have the plotter with her. Centennial to Pueblo by I-25, about 80 miles. There and back, 160. Over a hundred. She looked at it for a while, the way you look at a number on a monitor you've already decided you don't like.
A text from Jordan Reyes. What if the night cross-country is Pueblo. Sunday Dec 13. Down at 5:15, back at 9.
Abby answered at 11:10, which meant Abby was also awake for reasons.
A text from Abby Strand. Pueblo's 80. Round trip 160. It works on paper. What's in Pueblo.
A text from Jordan Reyes. My mom's birthday dinner. Danny always flew down.

Three dots for a long time. Then: Ok. Then you have a deadline and a reason, which is two more things than the airplane needs. We'll talk about that. Night one is Wednesday. Be at the hangar at 4:15. Before sunset. I mean it.
Claire texted at 11:30, because apparently nobody in her life slept. El wants to know if she can ride down in Biscuit with you. I said ask Aunt Jordan. I'm sorry.

She wrote back the rule, because it was easier than the rest of it. Training flights don't carry passengers. And when I'm alone, student pilots can't. Not even El. Claire sent back a picture of Ellie's face reading the text, which said everything about the regulation that needed saying.

Later, at two, with the rig restocked and nobody calling, she took the green notebook out of her flight bag and paged through the back half. She wasn't looking for anything. Then she was. December, five years ago. The first line said KPUB, and Ma, and a number that would have been her mother's age. She didn't read the rest. She folded the corner down, the way she'd done with his first cross-country, and put the notebook back in the bag. His, after hers. That was the rule.
Abby's Ground School: after dark, and when it goes wrong.
The regulations can't agree on when it's dark, so you're going to learn three answers and when each one applies. The test loves this, and so do examiners.

The first one is the definition. 14 CFR 1.1 says night is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. Civil twilight ends when the center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. Out here in late November that's about half an hour after sunset. On Wednesday the sun sets at 4:38 and civil twilight ends at 5:07. That's the night that counts for logging night time and for the night training your certificate requires.

The second one is for lights. 91.209 says that from sunset to sunrise you can't operate an aircraft unless its position lights are on. Sunset, not twilight. So at 4:39 on Wednesday the lights have to be on even though it isn't legally night yet.

The third one is for passengers. 61.57(b) says you can't act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise unless, within the preceding 90 days, you've made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during that same period, as the sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category and class. On Wednesday that window opens at 5:38. A landing at 5:20 counts as a night landing in your logbook and doesn't count for 61.57. A touch and go doesn't count for 61.57 at all. Full stop.

You won't need 61.57 until you have a certificate, because a student can't carry anybody. But you'll need it the first winter you want to bring Ellie home from somewhere after dinner, so learn it now, while it's free.

How the exam asks it. Expect three different questions with three different answers: the definition of night, when lights are required, and the period for passenger currency. 61.57(b) landings must be to a full stop.
What you need, and what you can't do.

61.109(a)(2) says your private certificate needs 3 hours of night flight training in a single-engine airplane, and that has to include one cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance and 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop, each one with a trip around the traffic pattern, at an airport. Training means me in the right seat. None of the night requirement for the private is solo.

Read that cross-country line carefully, because it's different from the one you flew alone. Over 100 nautical miles total distance. Pueblo and back by I-25 is about 160. For the hours to count as cross-country time under 61.1, the landing still has to be at a point more than 50 nautical miles straight line from where you started. Pueblo is 78.6.

Now the limits. On a dual flight I'm pilot in command, so 61.89 isn't what keeps Ellie home. I am. Training flights carry the trainee and the trainer, and that's it. 61.89 is for when you're PIC: as a student, no passengers, ever. Your mother wasn't going to ride along anyway, which I gather was never a risk. 61.89 also says a student can't be pilot in command with flight or surface visibility under 3 statute miles during the day or 5 at night, or when the flight can't be made with visual reference to the surface. Five at night. Remember the number. The night takes things away from you, and the rule asks for more room because of it.

Could you fly at night alone? Only after 61.87(o): night training at the airport you'll solo from, with takeoffs, approaches, landings, and go-arounds, and night navigation training near it, plus an endorsement for this make and model from the instructor who gave that training within the 90 days before the flight. The advisory circular has the wording, and it expires 90 days after the training. I'm not planning to give you that one. Your night is going to be with me.

How the exam asks it. The private needs 3 hours of night training with an instructor, including a cross-country over 100 NM total and 10 full-stop landings. A student acting as PIC carries no passengers, day or night.

91.205(c) is the night equipment list, and it sits on top of the day list you already know. Everything required for day VFR, plus approved position lights, an approved red or white anticollision light system, an electric landing light if the airplane is operated for hire, an adequate source of electrical energy for all the installed electrical and radio equipment, and one spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind, where the pilot can reach them in flight. People remember it as FLAPS: fuses, landing light if for hire, anticollision lights, position lights, a source of power. Biscuit has breakers, not fuses, so skip that letter. And the landing light's only required for hire. Nobody's paying me enough to count. We use it anyway.

Strobe dies in flight? 91.205 says you can keep going to somewhere it can get fixed. 91.209 lets you, the pilot in command, turn the strobes off when they're making things worse, like in haze, where they flash back in your face. Position lights don't get that deal. They're required, and 91.213 won't let you placard your way past anything 91.205 requires for the flight you're about to fly. Red light out on the left wing? Congratulations, you own a day airplane.

Same layout as a boat. Red on the left tip, green on the right tip, white on the tail. Here's the test question, straight out of the handbook. Another airplane's red is on your left and its green is on your right: it's headed the way you are. Keep your spacing. Red on your right, green on your left: that's its face. You might be about to meet. One white light by itself is somebody's tail, leaving.

The AFH wants landing lights on within 10 miles of an airport and below 10,000 feet, day or night. It also says to knock on every position light during the preflight. Blinks when you knock? Find out why before you leave.
How the exam asks it. Know the 91.205(c) additions for night, and the position light geometry. A question that shows red on the right, green on the left is asking you to recognize a head-on.

Beacons first. White, green, white, green: lighted civilian land airport. White and yellow: seaplane base, which you won't be needing. Military flashes two quick whites, then green. Ours turns from sunset to sunrise. Now and then you'll see one turning in broad daylight in a Class B, C, D or E surface area, and the AIM says that often means visibility under 3 or ceiling under 1,000, and you'd need a clearance. Then it says don't rely on the beacon alone. Classic AIM.

Runway edges are white. Instrument runways go yellow for the last 2,000 feet, or the last half if the runway's short, so you know you're running out. The end lights are two-faced. Green faces out, toward you on final, and that's the threshold. Red faces in, toward whoever's rolling out, and that's the end. Taxiway edges, blue. Taxiway centerlines, if they've got them, green. Outside the blue is ground nobody promised you anything about.

PAPI. Two or four lights in a row next to the runway, usually the left side. Four-light version: two white, two red, you're on the glide path. Three white, bit high. All white, high. Three red, bit low. All red, low, and low is the one with poles in it. The AIM gives you obstacle clearance within 10 degrees either side of centerline out to 3.4 miles, and it says don't start down on it until you're lined up. The older VASI is two bars. Red over white, you're all right. White over white, too high. Red over red, you're dead. Pilots made that one up, not me.

Some airports keep the lights off until you ask. That's pilot controlled lighting, on whatever frequency the Chart Supplement lists. Click the mic 7 times inside 5 seconds for high, 5 for medium, 3 for low. Seven first. Always seven first, says the AIM, because on some systems three won't wake up everything, and you can dial it down after. There's a 15 minute timer, and it restarts on your last click. Hit it again overhead or turning final. Otherwise the runway can shut off with you a hundred feet over the numbers. Yes, me. No, you can't have the story.
How the exam asks it. PAPI and VASI color questions are nearly free points. So is the 7, 5, 3 click sequence and the 15 minutes.

You know this better than I do, probably, but here's the pilot version. Cones: color, detail, packed into the middle of the retina, the fovea. Rods: dim light, no color, out in the edges. The handbook puts adapted rods at something like 10,000 times as sensitive as cones, which sounds great until you hear the catch. The fovea has no rods. So at night you've got a blind spot 5 to 10 degrees wide parked exactly where you point your eyes. Look right at a dim light, a tail light way out, and sometimes it's just gone.

Fix: look beside it. About 10 degrees off, above or below or to the side, whichever. And keep moving, because the PHAK says even that picture fades in 2 or 3 seconds if you hold still on it. For traffic, chop the sky into pieces, 10 degrees per piece at most, a second or more on each one. That's the AIM's version and it's a good one.

Getting your night eyes takes about half an hour for the whole set, per the AIM and both handbooks, or about 20 minutes to a decent amount under dim red light. Losing them takes one second of something bright. Ramp floodlight, somebody's landing light swinging across you on the taxiway: shut one eye. That one stays dark adapted and you'll be glad. Strobes are too quick to hurt it. Phones are not. You're going to dim your phone all the way and then dim it again.

Red light keeps your adaptation, and it ruins your chart. Under red light, magenta washes out into the paper and blue things go dark, and half of what's printed on a sectional is magenta. The AFH's answer is a flashlight with both a red and a white light: white for the walkaround, red in the cockpit, dim white when you need to read the chart. Bring two, and spare batteries.

Things that make night vision worse: altitude, because the AIM says it's impaired above about 5,000 feet of cabin altitude and Centennial is 5,885, which is why the books recommend oxygen above 5,000 at night. Carbon monoxide, including from smoking. Low vitamin A. Prolonged bright sun earlier in the day. My rule, not the book's: if you're flying tonight, wear sunglasses all day. And everything on IMSAFE, especially fatigue.
How the exam asks it. Expect off-center viewing, 30 minutes of dark adaptation, and the 5,000 foot night oxygen recommendation. "Look directly at it" is never the right answer at night.
You met most of the illusions in the human factors chapter. Night brings out the ones that only need your eyes to fool you.

False horizon. Ground lights and stars smeared together, or a tilted line of lights, and your brain grabs the wrong line and calls it level. Out east, a road going up a hill will do it to you every time. You'll drop a wing to match and feel great about it. Autokinesis. Stare at one light on a dark background, and after 8 or 10 seconds it starts wandering around. People have followed it into the dirt. Same cure for both. Keep your eyes moving, and when outside stops making sense, fly the attitude indicator.

Landing ones. Featureless ground under final, like water, a dark field, snow, makes you feel high, so you come in low. That's the black hole approach: runway lights, and under you, nothing. Bright runway lights with dark all around make the runway seem closer, so you come in high. A straight row of lights on a road, or a train, can pass for a runway. Rain on the windshield, you feel high. Haze, the runway looks far off. Rule of thumb: whatever makes you feel high makes you fly low. And low is where the poles live.

Flicker vertigo is the weird one. Light flickering 4 to 20 times a second, a strobe chopped up by the prop, say, can make some people dizzy or sick or worse. Something flickering at you? Make it stop.

Fixing it is boring. Use the PAPI. Look at the altimeter on every approach. Learn the airport before you show up, from the Chart Supplement, and if you can, from flying it in daylight first. And the AFH says a low, shallow approach is definitely inappropriate at night. Definitely. I'd take the hint.
How the exam asks it. Featureless terrain and darkness produce a low approach. Bright lights produce a high one. Autokinesis comes from staring at a single light.
The airplane doesn't know it's dark. Everything about how it flies is the same. What changes is you, and what you can see, so the procedures lean harder on the instruments.

Preflight by daylight when you can. Check every light, tap the position lights, and walk the ramp with the flashlight for chocks, ladders, and tie down ropes. Organize the cockpit before you start: flashlight where your hand can find it, chart folded, checklist out. Clear the propeller area with extra care and turn the beacon on so anybody nearby knows. Taxi slowly. In the run-up, hold the brakes and watch for creeping, because at night you won't notice the airplane rolling forward until it's on the hold line.

On takeoff, the runway lights keep you straight, and then they're behind you and there's nothing ahead. Fly the attitude indicator, the altimeter, and the vertical speed indicator until they all agree you're climbing. The AFH says inexperienced pilots sometimes relax right rudder after liftoff and drift left, and that you shouldn't turn until you're at a safe altitude. Turn the landing light off once the climb is established if it's reflecting off haze.

In cruise, you can't see clouds at night. The AFH says the first sign is usually the ground lights fading out. If they start to get halos, that's moisture, and going on in the same direction calls for caution. The handbook's summary of the whole chapter is the sentence I want you to remember: even for experienced pilots, night VFR should only be flown in unrestricted visibility, favorable winds on the surface and aloft, and no turbulence. Even for experienced pilots.

On approach, find the beacon and fly toward it until you can pick out the runway lights from everything else. Fly a normal pattern at normal speeds, cross-check the altimeter on every leg, and use the PAPI. Landing light on about halfway down final. Start the round out when the light shows you the tire marks on the runway. If the landing light fails, start the round out when the lights at the far end of the runway appear to rise above the nose, and feel for the runway with a little power. We'll practice that one. The AFH says blackout landings belong in every night pilot's training.
How the exam asks it. Night takeoffs lean on the flight instruments. The first sign of cloud at night is ground lights disappearing.

Fly the airplane first. Always, day or night. Pitch for best glide, trim for it, and then think. Biscuit's best glide is 65 knots indicated, flaps up. The club's glide card says that from 1,000 feet above the ground, in still air, she'll go about a mile and a half, which is roughly 9 to 1. A headwind takes some of that away and a tailwind gives some back, in proportion to what it does to your groundspeed. Best glide is the speed for the most distance. Minimum sink is a little slower and keeps you in the air the longest, but covers less ground. If you need to get somewhere, fly best glide.

Then the handbook's terms. A forced landing is immediate, because you can't keep flying, like an engine failure. A precautionary landing is one you choose when you still could keep flying but shouldn't, for weather, fuel, being lost, or an engine running rough. The AFH warns that too many precautionary landings turn into forced ones because the pilot used wishful thinking instead of reason. The noninstrument pilot trapped by weather is the example it uses.

Picking a place. Height decides how much choice you have. From high up, pick a general area first and then a spot. The handbook says you can discard a plan for one that's obviously better, and that you shouldn't change your mind more than once. A well-flown landing in poor terrain beats an uncontrolled one in a perfect field. Land into the wind if you can, at the slowest speed you can control, because doubling your groundspeed quadruples the energy that has to go somewhere. Let the airplane's wings and gear absorb it. The airplane is the dispensable part. Roads look tempting, and most of them have power lines along them that you won't see until late.

At night the AFH adds a list. Keep control and set up best glide. Turn toward an airport, or away from built up areas. Look for the cause: fuel selector, mixture, magnetos, primer. Tell ATC, and if you're already talking to someone, don't change frequencies unless they say to. If you know the terrain, plan for an unlighted part of it, close to a road or public access if you can, so help can get to you. Know the wind. Run the before landing checklist, test the landing light at altitude, and turn it on in time to see what's ahead. If you have no light and no outside reference, hold a level landing attitude until you touch. Then switches off and get out.

Partial power is more common than total. Roughness in the O-320 on a cool, damp night is carb ice until proven otherwise, so carb heat on and leave it on. Then the fuel selector, the mixture, the mags one at a time, and the primer locked. A sick engine that's still making some power is a gift. Use it to get to a better field, and plan the landing like it might quit on final.
How the exam asks it. Expect best glide versus minimum sink, the effect of wind on glide distance, and forced versus precautionary landing.

Engine fire in flight. The AFH says unless the manufacturer says otherwise, the first step is to shut off the fuel: mixture to idle cutoff, fuel selector off. Leave the ignition on so the engine burns what's left in the lines. If the fire goes out, don't restart. Then you're gliding, and you know what to do. Some checklists say master off too. Biscuit's has it third, which is why your mayday goes out before you get there. The handbook points out that unless it's an electrical fire or you're about to touch down, that also kills your radios and your transponder. A single-engine airplane with an engine fire is landing, and soon, and the handbook's line is the right one: the airplane is expendable, and the only thing that matters is the people in it. An emergency descent, if you need one, is power idle and a bank of about 30 to 45 degrees to keep the wings loaded, within the airplane's speed limits.

Electrical fire smells like hot insulation. Try to find the circuit by checking breakers and switches. If you can't, and the flying allows it, master and alternator off. If you really need power, the handbook gives a way to find the bad circuit, and then says the most prudent thing is to land as soon as possible.

Cabin fire: use the extinguisher first, and only then open the vents to clear the smoke. Opening the vents first feeds it, and if the smoke gets worse when you open them, close them. Biscuit's extinguisher clips under the left seat. Know how to pull the pin without looking.

Alternator failure, which Marisol asked you about in May. The ammeter shows a steady discharge, the needle sitting left of center by about what the airplane is drawing, a few amps up to maybe twenty, and now the battery's carrying everything. The AFH's example is a 25 amp hour battery that might give 5 amps for 5 hours, or only about 10 to 15 minutes at 40 amps, and less if it's old. So shed everything you don't need, right away. Tell ATC. Land at the nearest suitable airport. At night, nearest suitable means lit and open, and if the lights are on a radio switch, it means one where you'll still have a radio when you get there.
How the exam asks it. The first action for an in-flight engine fire is to shut off fuel to the engine. For an alternator failure, it's reducing the electrical load.

The AIM has a sentence I'd like on your wall. An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or any other condition that could hurt the flight. Doubtful. Not sure you're in trouble. Doubtful. That's the time to ask, before it's a distress. The AIM says delay has caused accidents and cost lives.

Distress is MAYDAY, urgency is PAN-PAN, each said three times if you can. Then who you're calling, who you are, what's wrong, the weather, what you want, where you are, your altitude, fuel in minutes, and people aboard. If you're already talking to a controller and have a code, keep it unless they tell you otherwise, because they already know where you are. If you can't reach anyone, squawk 7700, and keep calling. You know 7600 and 7500 from the last chapter. 91.3 says the pilot in command may deviate from the rules as much as an emergency requires, and send a written report if the FAA asks. Nobody's going to violate you for saving your own life.

There's one frequency that military towers, most civil towers and radar facilities listen to, called the emergency frequency, and you'll find it in the Chart Supplement. Direction finding stations listen to it too. If the frequency you're on goes quiet, that's the next one to try.

ELTs. The old analog kind broadcasts a swept tone on the emergency frequency. Satellites stopped listening for those in 2009, so now an analog ELT depends on someone nearby hearing it. The newer digital kind talks to the satellites, carries the owner's information, and has to be registered with NOAA, and search and rescue reacts to it much faster. Look at the label on Biscuit's and tell me which she has. Analog ELTs get tested only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps at most, and never in the air. Before you shut down after a hard landing, or any landing, listen on the emergency frequency for a second to make sure yours didn't go off. 91.207 has the battery rules you met in May: replace it after an hour of cumulative use or half its useful life, and inspect the ELT every 12 calendar months.

And if you ever lose the ground at night, in a cloud or a snow shower, the AFH says the only concern is keeping the wings level. Fly the attitude indicator, gently, with your fingertips. Untrained pilots lose control in about 10 minutes on instruments alone. Tell ATC you aren't instrument rated and declare the emergency. The PHAK's advice for preventing it is the reason this chapter has the title it has: decide early to turn around and land at an alternate with better weather, and always consider safer alternatives rather than hope things work out.
How the exam asks it. Urgency starts at doubt. Already talking to ATC, keep your code. Analog ELT tests in the first 5 minutes of the hour.
Night fuel, and the night you don't go.

91.151(a)(2) is the night half of the fuel rule. You can't begin a VFR flight in an airplane unless, considering the wind and forecast weather, you have enough fuel to fly to your first point of intended landing and then fly at normal cruise for at least 45 minutes at night. Forty five instead of thirty, because at night the alternate is farther away in every sense. At 8 gallons an hour, that's 6 gallons. The club's land with an hour still applies. Walt has his own number, and he'll tell you.

91.103 already makes you think about alternatives before you leave. At night they shrink. A field you'd happily land in at noon is a dark rectangle at nine. An airport with lights on a radio switch is an airport where you need a radio. A cross-country at night is planned around lit airports, roads you can follow, and the highest terrain you'll cross, and the PHAK suggests flying the route by day first and deciding the lowest altitude you're willing to accept at night. If the weather won't let you hold that altitude, you turn around early.

The last thing in this chapter is the one the test asks about least and you'll use most. The AFH says the greatest worry in a single-engine airplane at night is an engine failure, and then it says, quietly, that continuing into adverse weather and poor judgment cause most of the serious accidents. The engine almost never quits. People almost always keep going. External pressure, a dinner, a family waiting, a deadline, is the thing you learned to name last month. The way you handle it is to decide what turns you around before you're in the car, and then to let it.
How the exam asks it. Night reserve is 45 minutes. Calculation questions give a burn and a time and ask for total fuel with the night reserve.

Wednesday, November 25, 4:15 PM, the ramp. Low sun on the foothills. The hangar shadows reached clear across the taxiway and onto the grass. Jordan had slept until one. Thursday at seven she was back at the station for Thanksgiving, which on an ambulance is a normal shift plus a pie somebody's mother drops off at the bay door around noon.

Abby came out of the office with two flashlights. One was the size of a baguette, with a red lens on a little hinge that flipped down over the white one. The other hung on a lanyard and smelled faintly of Abby's car, which was coffee and old fries.

Sunset's 4:38. Twilight ends 5:07. We take off before that and land after, which is the point of tonight. Six full stops. And the examiner is going to ask you what you did with the next half hour, so.
She checked her watch. Looked at the sky. Looked at Jordan.
A. Preflight now while it's light, then sit in the dim cockpit and let her eyes adjust.
B. Preflight now while it's light, then wait in the FBO with a coffee until it's time to start.
C. Skip checking the lights tonight. Russ flew her Saturday, and he'd have said something if one was out.
D. Wait for full dark and do the preflight with her phone's flashlight, so her eyes have adjusted by takeoff.

She does the walkaround with the white light anyway, for the practice, while there's still daylight to check it against. Master on. Beacon, strobes, landing light. Red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white on the tail. Abby shows her the knuckle tap on each position light, and none of them so much as blink. Then she climbs in, turns the panel lights down to a dull orange, flips the red lens over, and sits. Abby sits. Nobody talks. Ten minutes in, the ramp starts coming back to her in grays, tie down rings, chocks, a gas cap somebody left sitting on a wing two rows over. There. Night eyes. Now don't look at your phone. I mean it. It's a flashlight with opinions.

That's it. The AFH recommends checking every light during the preflight and tapping the position light fixtures. Full dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes, moderate adaptation about 20 under dim red light, and any bright light for a second or more costs some of it.
Decision two. Stars and ranch lights.

First takeoff at 4:58, into a sky the color of a bruise. First landing at 5:05, technically a day landing, though it didn't feel like one. By the third takeoff it was night by the logbook's definition. Off three five right and right for the downwind, the runway slid back under the wing, and then there was nothing in the windshield at all.

East, out the left window, the subdivisions just stopped, like somebody had run out of houses. Past them was the plains, black, with ranch lights sprinkled on it here and there, and above the ranch lights, stars, and it was hard to say exactly where one bunch quit and the other started. The moon was coming up too. Huge, orange, ninety eight percent, sitting on the ground like a dropped plate.
Off the wing a string of headlights ran uphill across her window. She rolled level with it. Felt fine.
A. Look out again and find the moon. It's sitting right on the horizon, so she can level the wings against it.
B. Keep flying by the lights outside, and check the instruments every few seconds to stay honest.
C. Level the wings on the attitude indicator, check the altimeter, and use outside only for traffic.
D. Ask Abby to take the airplane for a minute until her eyes adjust to the picture.

Attitude indicator. Ten degrees of right bank she hadn't felt and hadn't asked for. She rolls level, checks 6,900 on the altimeter, and right away the airplane swears to her it's banking left. She lets it swear. That's the road. Road's on a hill. Classic false horizon, and you'll get it every single time you turn east out here. Jordan says it out loud so it'll stick. Road's on a hill. Get it printed on a mug.

Yep. That's the one. A dark scene with ground lights and stars, or a line of lights on sloping ground, can create a false horizon. The fix is the flight instruments for attitude, with the outside scan for traffic.

Fourth landing. Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared to land. She read it back. On base the approach lights were doing their thing, a little white rabbit running at the runway over and over, and the runway was a pair of white rows with a green bar at her end. Left side, a bit down, the PAPI.
Problem was, it looked right there. She'd hung on to her altitude on base an extra few seconds because of that, and now on final the PAPI said three white and one red. Then four white.
10,000 feet of runway. Abby had her chin on her fist and was looking out her side like she was thinking about lunch.
A. Go around and set up a better approach from the start.
B. Ease the power back, hold 65 knots, and let it settle to two white and two red.
C. Push the nose over to get down to the glide path fast, then level off when the lights turn red.
D. Ignore the PAPI. She can see the runway fine, and with ten thousand feet she'll have room.

Little high. So fix it. She takes a hundred RPM out and leaves 65 where it is, and Biscuit sinks a bit, and the box goes three white and then two and two. There. Now quit touching it. Jordan puts the hundred back. Then she waits for the landing light to find the tire marks. It takes forever. Black rubber, finally, smeared across the white, and she starts the round out. On the rollout Abby says, Bright runway, dark ground. Gets everybody. Got me at Grand Junction my first winter, and I had eight hundred hours.

Exactly right. Three white and one red is slightly high on a four-light PAPI. A small power reduction at constant airspeed captures the glide path. AFH: round out when the landing light shows the tire marks on the runway.

After the first night she'd added a line to the bottom of the card on the panel, smaller than the rest because she was out of room. NIGHT: DUAL ONLY. CEILING 5,000 AGL ALL THE WAY. NO SNOW. NO RIDGES UNDER A LOWERING DECK. IF THE LIGHTS GO FUZZY, TURN AROUND.

Thursday, December 3, 7:40 PM. Night two. She'd come off a shift at seven that morning and slept until two, and had decided, out loud, in her kitchen, that she was fine, and had then made herself answer every letter of IMSAFE before she believed it. No moon tonight. It wouldn't be up until almost three in the morning. Abby had picked the night on purpose.

It was minus six on the ramp. Light leaked out where the hangar door didn't quite meet the frame. Inside, somebody was singing with the radio, badly. Marisol, then, fixing something that wasn't broken.

On the walkaround, master on, Jordan tapped the red light on the left wingtip with one knuckle, the way she had the first night. It went out. She tapped it again. It came on. Again. Out. It stayed out.
A. Ask Marisol to fix it and sign for it, then tap it again herself before they go.
B. Go. One position light is a small thing, and the strobes and the beacon make her plenty visible.
C. Cancel the lesson and write the light up on the squawk list for Marisol in the morning.
D. Placard it inoperative under 91.213 and stay in the pattern tonight, close to the airport.

Marisol comes out in a headlamp with a spare bulb held in her teeth. The screwdriver comes out of a pocket Jordan didn't know the coveralls had. Two screws, lens off. The old bulb is scorched black on one side and the contact has gone fuzzy green. There's your blink. A wire brush, a new bulb, and then Jordan has to knock on it ten times while Marisol counts out loud. It stays on. Then the logbook, under the hangar light: date, tach time, lamp replaced, socket cleaned, signature, and the pencil goes back behind her ear. Danny tapped them too. Said the airplane would tell you things if you knocked.

That's it. The AFH recommends tapping position light fixtures during the night preflight and finding the cause of any flicker before flight. Position lights are required for night VFR, so the fix and the maintenance record come before takeoff.

8:31 PM, the practice area just north of Bennett, about twenty miles northeast of Centennial, 7,500 feet. The ground out here was about 5,500 feet and almost entirely invisible. There were the lights of Bennett off to the south, a gas station on I-70, and a county road running north and south below them with a farm light at every mile like beads. Between the beads, nothing. Fields, presumably.

Abby had shown her the winds before they left: about 15 knots out of the north at this altitude. She'd also, earlier, made Jordan read the glide card taped inside the POH cover, Marisol's capitals on an index card: BEST GLIDE 65 KIAS. FLAPS UP. 1.5 NM PER 1,000 FT AGL, NO WIND.
Abby reached over and pulled the throttle to idle.
Engine failure. Talk to me. We stop at 6,500, a thousand above the ground, and go home.
A. Pitch for 65 and head straight for Centennial. Holding the nose up a little will stretch the glide.
B. Pitch for 65, turn toward the dark field just north of the lit county road, into the wind, then the checklist.
C. Pitch for 65, then turn toward the darkest field she can see, the one farthest from anything.
D. Pitch for 65 and turn toward the lights of Bennett, so she can see what she's landing on.

Nose up, trim, 65. She puts the field off the nose, a dark rectangle a mile and change north with a farm light at its corner and the road running down its west side. Into the wind. Fuel selector both, mixture rich, carb heat on, mags both, primer in and locked. Nothing changes, because Abby's hand is on the throttle. Mayday, mayday, mayday, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, engine failure, twenty miles northeast of Centennial, landing in a field. She says it to the windshield, not the radio. Landing light on at 6,800 to test it. The beam goes out and finds nothing. At 6,500 Abby pushes the throttle in and the engine roars back like it was offended. You'd have made it. You'd have seen the stubble in time from about two hundred feet. That's all a landing light gives you.

Yep. That's the one. AFH night engine failure: best glide, toward an unlighted area of known terrain near public access, into the wind, check the causes, announce the emergency, and use the landing light in time to see the terrain. Avoid the road itself, which may have wires.

9:08 PM. The Space Port's tower had closed at nine, and the airport sat out on the plains ahead of them inside the Bravo's notch, under the 70, its beacon turning white and green, white and green, and below it nothing. No runway. A black hole where an eight thousand foot runway was supposed to be.

Jordan had the Chart Supplement entry on her kneeboard, copied the night before. The runway lights were on a radio switch now, on the airport's common frequency, which she'd already tuned. She'd announced herself on it, eight miles east, inbound for runway 26.
Abby had her hands in her lap.
A. Land on the landing light and the GPS. The runway is eight thousand feet long and right where the box says.
B. Call the tower and ask them to turn the runway lights on for her arrival.
C. Key the mic seven times within five seconds, then check that the edge lights and the PAPI came on.
D. Key it three times for the lowest setting, so the runway lights don't wreck her night vision.

Click click click click click click click. The runway comes on all at once, two long lines of white drawn on the dark, the threshold green, and a pair of lights to the left of the near end, one red, one white. Two-light PAPI. One and one is on path. Write down the time. 9:08. Fifteen minutes from now they go out whether you're on final or not. Key them again on downwind. She does, at 9:15, and again on the next downwind, without being told.

Exactly right. AIM 2-1-8: key the microphone 7 times within 5 seconds to turn on all controlled lights at maximum intensity, adjust lower with 5 or 3 if desired. Lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation, so key again near the field.

9:36 PM. Three miles west of the Space Port, climbing for home under the 70. Behind them the runway lights were still on, burning down the last of their fifteen minutes. Abby reached across and flipped the ALT half of the master off.
The ammeter needle slid left of center and stayed there, a steady discharge.
Alternator's dead. You're on the battery. Go.
Back in May, on a Saturday, with the cowling off and Marisol not looking up from her wire, Jordan had answered this exact question, a night flight over Limon. Easier with your feet on concrete.
A. Shed load and keep heading home. Centennial is twelve minutes, and the battery should last that.
B. Turn the whole master off to save the battery for later, and fly home on the flashlight.
C. Pull the circuit breakers one at a time to find which circuit is causing it, then decide.
D. Shed everything she doesn't need, tell Approach, and go back to the Space Port while it's lit.

Landing light off. GPS off. The second radio off. Panel lights down to the least she can read. She keeps one radio and the transponder. Denver Approach, Niner One Echo, alternator failure, returning to the Space Port, three miles west. She banks back east and the runway is right there, still lit, a minute or two left on its timer. She keys it again, seven clicks, on downwind. Abby flips the ALT back on as they turn final, because it's training and the landing light makes the landing easier to grade. Nearest suitable. At night that means lit. You picked the one you'd just keyed. That's the whole lesson.

That's it. AFH: after a generating system failure, immediately shed nonessential loads, notify ATC, and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport. Keep what you need for communication and the landing, including what it takes to activate the lights.

Monday, December 7, eleven in the morning, the hangar. Biscuit's cowling was off again. Marisol called it an oil seep. Walt, walking through with a coffee, called it a hobby. Jordan's logbook said 3.6 hours of night now and ten night landings, five from the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and five from last Thursday. One box left. The cross-country.
Marisol had the little red extinguisher out from under the left seat and was reading it. The gauge, the date, the fine print, all of it, the way some people read a cereal box at breakfast.

Pop quiz. Night, 7,500, out over the plains. You smell something hot. Then smoke out the bottom of the cowling, right here, and she pointed the extinguisher at the bottom of the engine, at the exhaust pipes and the fuel lines, and there's light under it, and it's not your landing light. It's orange. What do your hands do first?
A. Open the windows and vents to clear the smoke, so she can see to fly.
B. Dive steeply at full speed to try to blow the fire out, then pull out and land at the nearest airport.
C. Master switch off first, so there's no electrical power anywhere in the airplane to feed it.
D. Mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector off, ignition left on, then set up for a forced landing.

Yep. She reaches in and pulls the mixture all the way out to show her, then puts a boot on the fuel selector on the floor, the sticky one. All the way to OFF, and feel it seat. She's the one that hangs up short of BOTH, so don't trust your hand, trust the click. Do it blind a few times. Mags? The AFH says leave them on so the engine burns off what's in the lines. Biscuit's checklist doesn't mention them. If the fire goes out, it stays out. No restart. Biscuit's checklist says master off third, so make your mayday before you get there. Then you're a glider, with a story. She sets the extinguisher on the wing. This one's for the cabin. Pin, aim low at the base, squeeze, sweep. Then crack a vent, because the stuff in there isn't great to breathe either.

Yep. That's the one. AFH engine fire procedure, unless the POH directs otherwise: shut off fuel with the mixture at idle cutoff and the fuel selector off, leave the ignition on to burn the fuel in the lines, don't restart, and make a forced landing.
Decision nine. The number you don't plan to.
Thursday, December 10, four in the afternoon, the briefing room. The Pueblo nav log was done, two pages in pencil, and Walt had asked to see it, which Walt didn't do.

He'd read her November fuel column once already and initialed it. He read this one the way he'd read release paperwork for thirty years, one finger moving down the page, glasses on the end of his nose. Night's different. You know the rule. I want to hear what you plan.

Her log said 80 miles each way by I-25, 118 knots south with the forecast tailwind and 92 coming home into it, 8 gallons an hour, a gallon for taxi and a gallon for the climb at each end. Biscuit's tanks held 40 usable.
What do you land with? And where's your alternate on the way home?
A. Fill it, and skip planning an alternate. With 40 gallons aboard, fuel isn't going to be the problem.
B. Full tanks, and enough coming home to turn around at Monument, go back to Pueblo, and still have 45 minutes.
C. Leave with half tanks to save weight, and top off at Pueblo after dinner from the self-serve pump.
D. Plan the 30 minute day reserve. She takes off before full dark, and the rule goes by when you begin.

She shows him the bottom of the page, where she'd already done it. Full tanks, 40. Pueblo with about 32. Home with about 23 if nothing goes wrong. And the line she'd written for him, because she knew he'd ask: if the Divide is down coming home, Pueblo to Monument and back to Pueblo, plus 45, is about 16 gallons, and she'd leave Pueblo with 32. Walt reads it twice. Then he takes a pen out of his jacket and, under her numbers, in small square capitals, writes RELEASED. W.H. Old habit. That's the number I'd have wanted on a release.

Exactly right. A dispatcher's fuel plan covers the destination, an alternate, and the reserve. Planning the return so a turnaround at the worst point still leaves the 91.151 night reserve is the ACS fuel planning risk element done properly.

Sunday, December 13, 8:50 in the morning, her kitchen. Her mother's birthday. She'd texted happy birthday at 7:01 and gotten back Thank you mija. Drive safe if you drive., which was her mother's way of saying a great many things.

Weather, printed at 8:44 AM. METAR KAPA 131453Z 34006KT 10SM SCT120 M03/M11 A3024 RMK AO2. TAF KAPA 131120Z 1312/1412 34008KT P6SM SCT120. FM132100 36010KT P6SM BKN080. FM140400 03012KT 4SM -SN BR OVC025. FM140900 03010KT 2SM -SN BR OVC012. TAF KPUB 131120Z 1312/1412 32008KT P6SM FEW120. FM140200 34010KT P6SM SCT080. FB DEN 9000 3413-08. NOTES OFF THE GFA GRAPHIC, FRONT RANGE AND PALMER DIVIDE: UPSLOPE DEVELOPING THIS EVENING BEHIND A COLD FRONT. CIG LWRG TO 1000-2500 AGL AND -SN, EARLIEST OVER THE PALMER DIVIDE. TIMING UNCERTAIN.

She did the conversion out loud. Zero four hundred Zulu on the 14th, minus seven, is nine o'clock tonight. Her plan had her leaving Pueblo at 8:40 and landing at Centennial at about 9:35. Right into it.
And the graphical forecast said the Divide went first. Timing uncertain.
The night line on the card over the mag switch said 5,000 AGL all the way. She'd written it after the first night, when nothing was riding on it.
A. Fly down as planned, and if the return looks bad from Pueblo, leave Biscuit there and ride home with Claire.
B. Cancel the flight now. A front at night is a front at night, and she'd rather decide it over coffee.
C. Set a go or no-go time of 4:45 on the newest weather, with the Divide written as the test, and the car as plan B.
D. Keep the plan but leave Pueblo by eight instead of 8:40, so she's home before it comes in at nine.

She writes it on the nav log in red before she can talk herself out of it. 4:45 PM, NEWEST TAF, METARS, PIREPS. DIVIDE CEILING PER THE CARD, ALL THE WAY, BOTH WAYS. IF NOT, I DRIVE. LEAVE BY 5:15 EITHER WAY. She takes a picture and sends it to Abby, who sends back a thumbs up and then, a minute later, Also put the cake in your car now. Either way.

That's it. The PHAK and RMH recommend setting decision criteria before the pressure arrives. A decision point on the latest data, a specific weather test for the critical terrain, and a ready alternative are what make a no-go easy to carry out.
Decision eleven. Face up on the table.
1:40 PM, and her mother called. Called, not texted. Jordan watched the screen through two rings before she picked up.

Claire says you're going to fly to my dinner. A pause. Your brother always flew. Every year I sat in the back room at Velarde's with my phone on the table, face up, next to the bread, and every year the waiters knew not to move it. Another pause, longer. I'm not telling you not to come. I want you there. I'm telling you about the phone.

Behind her mother's voice she could hear Claire's kitchen, a cabinet banging, Ellie somewhere asking something about whether there'd be the flan with the burnt part. They were leaving at three. Ellie had made a sign. Jordan knew about the sign because Ellie had sent her a picture of it at noon: WELCOME TO PUEBLO AUNT JORDAN, in purple, with an airplane on it that was clearly Biscuit, because the 4 in the tail number was backward.
Claire had texted underneath the picture. She wants to watch you land. I told her maybe.
A. Tell her mother and Claire now that she might drive, she decides at 4:45, and she'll be there.
B. Don't mention the weather to her mother. It'll only worry her, and it may not matter.
C. Tell her mother she's driving, period, so nobody has to worry and the call can be over.
D. Promise Ellie she'll see the landing at six. It'll give the kid something good to look forward to.

Ma. I might drive. Weather's coming over the Divide tonight, and I decide at quarter to five. Either way I'm there. If I drive I'm late, and I'll call when I leave. The line goes quiet. Then: Okay. Then, in a voice Jordan hasn't heard out of her since high school: Your brother never once told me maybe. Same text to Claire, plus: tell El the sign works for a car. Claire: Told her. She's adding a car. It has like nine wheels.

Yep. That's the one. The PHAK lists managing passengers' and other people's expectations as a key way to manage external pressure. Telling the people waiting ahead of time that she might be late or drive takes away the pressure to make the flight happen.

4:45 PM. Biscuit's left seat, at the tie down, preflight done in the last of the light, every light tapped twice, the tanks topped to the filler necks. Abby in the right seat with the iPad on her knee. Overhead, the overcast was high and still gray-white. To the south, over the Palmer Divide, it wasn't. It was a flat gray lid sitting low on the ridgeline, and the ridgeline was gone under it in places.

Weather, printed at 4:41 PM. METAR KAPA 132253Z 36010KT 10SM BKN050 OVC070 M02/M08 A3027 RMK AO2. METAR KCOS 132254Z 01012KT 5SM -SN BR OVC028 M03/M05 A3028. METAR KPUB 132253Z 33009KT 10SM SCT080 01/M07 A3022. TAF KAPA 132320Z AMD 1323/1418 36010KT P6SM BKN050. FM140100 03012KT 4SM -SN BR OVC020. FM140400 03012KT 1 1/2SM -SN BR OVC008. UA /OV BRK360010/TM 2320/FL085/TP C182/SK OVC100/WX FV04SM -SN/RM CIG LWRG RAPIDLY. TERRAIN OBSC E OF I-25.

She did the arithmetic out loud, the way she'd do a dose. The amended TAF brought the lowering at Centennial from nine o'clock to six. The PIREP was from a Skylane twenty five minutes ago, ten miles north of the Black Forest VOR, right over the top of the Divide: overcast at 10,000, flight visibility four in light snow, ceiling lowering rapidly. The ground under that airplane was about 7,500 feet. Twenty five hundred feet between the ridge and the clouds, and getting smaller. Colorado Springs had a 2,800 foot overcast and snow. Pueblo was fine. Pueblo was always going to be fine.

She looked at the card above the mag switch, at the small line she'd squeezed in at the bottom after the first night. CEILING 5,000 AGL ALL THE WAY. NO SNOW. NO RIDGES UNDER A LOWERING DECK. And above it, in bigger letters, the line she'd written in November. I DON'T CHANGE THIS CARD IN THE PARKING LOT.
Your call tonight, Abby said. It's legal right now, every piece of it. I'll fly what you decide. I'll tell you afterward what I'd have done.
A. Fly the east side of the Divide instead, out by Kiowa and Calhan, where the ground is lower.
B. Go now. Centennial is VFR, the lowering is an hour out, and she'll be past the Divide by 5:35.
C. Wait at the FBO until six, and decide once the next round of METARs shows which way it's going.
D. Drive. Tell Abby, call Claire, and leave now, before the snow reaches Monument Hill.

No. It comes out easier than she expected, and quieter. The Divide's at 2,500 and dropping. That's not a number I'm crossing at night. I'm driving. Abby nods once, short, the nod she saves for a good checklist, and starts unbuckling. I'd have said no at four. I wanted to hear you say it. Jordan calls Claire from the cockpit, and Claire says Okay. I'll tell her. Drive safe, the pass is getting bad, and somewhere behind her Ellie shouts something about the car part of the sign.

Exactly right. The PIREP showed ceilings lowering rapidly over the highest terrain on the route, the TAF had been amended earlier, and it was night. The AFH says night VFR belongs in unrestricted visibility. Deciding on the ground, with a ready alternative, is the decision the whole chapter has been building.

Abby walked her to the hangar. Neither of them said anything about the flight that wasn't going to happen, which Jordan understood was a kind of respect. The tanks were full. They'd stay full. Russ had Biscuit Monday, and Russ would be delighted.

Walt was in the hangar. He hadn't said he'd be there. He was sitting on Marisol's rolling stool, which Jordan had never seen anybody but Marisol sit on, in his canvas jacket with two coffees from the FBO on the workbench beside him and his reading glasses folded in his shirt pocket. He'd been watching the weather on his phone, the way he must have watched it for thirty years, and he'd seen the PIREP. He'd known it was her night. He held out one of the coffees.

You're not going, he said. It wasn't a question, and he didn't sound pleased or surprised. He sounded like a man who'd been waiting at a gate to see which way somebody would walk. Sit down a minute before you drive. There's something I've been not telling you since April.
She sat on an upturned bucket. Walt looked at the coffee instead of at her.

Winter of ninety six. I was thirty four. Two years on the desk at a regional outfit that doesn't exist anymore. A thirty-some seat turboprop, eleven people in the back. A night run into a mountain town I'm not going to name. The forecast at the destination was above minimums, with snow showers in the vicinity. Legal. The alternate was legal. The fuel was legal, and then some. On an airline, the captain and the dispatcher both sign the release. Both of us own it.

I had a feeling about those showers. I didn't have a reason. I had a feeling, and a forecast that said yes, and a station that kept calling because there were people waiting for a wedding. So I signed. The captain signed. He turned the cup a quarter turn on the bench. They didn't come home.
The hangar heater ticked. Somewhere outside, a truck went by on the service road with its chains on.

The report said what those reports say. It talked about the descent and the snow and the terrain. It didn't have my name in it. It didn't need to. The release did. He finally looked at her. I've spent thirty years since then telling people things they didn't want to hear about the weather. I told myself it was the job. It was the eleven people. The forecast is permission. That's all it ever is. I treated it like a reason.

I wanted the share sold because I didn't think you'd be able to do what you just did. Most people can't. Most pilots can't. Your brother couldn't, and I loved your brother. He stood, slowly, the way he did everything. You turned it down with the tanks full and your family waiting. I've spent thirty years waiting to see somebody do that without me telling them to.
He picked up his coffee and went out the side door to his truck, and didn't look back, and Jordan understood that was the only way he could have said any of it.

Car running, heater on high and doing nothing yet, snow collecting in the corners of the windshield where the wipers didn't reach. She dug the green notebook out of her flight bag. Folded corner. His, after hers. She'd made her call, so now he got his.

Danny's logbook, a page from December, five years ago. Dec 11. KPUB to KAPA, night. 1.1 on the Hobbs. Ma's 58th at Velarde's. Left at 9:40 because Tia wouldn't stop bringing flan.. TAF said the snow came after midnight. It came at ten. By Pueblo it was nothing, by the Springs it was low, by Monument it was the road. Followed the I-25 headlights over the hill at what I am going to write down as 800 feet and was not 800 feet. Lost the ground. I don't know how long. Long enough to know what it feels like. Came out over Larkspur with the wings level only because I was too scared to move them.. Landed. Sat in the car an hour with the engine running. Called Ma from the car and told her it was a beautiful night.. Got lucky. Never again. Don't tell Mom.. (Next year leave Velarde's by 7. Beat it home.)

Twice through. Then the parentheses again, because of course. Never again, and one line down, how to keep doing it anyway. Leave by 7, beat it home. Every year after that he left a little earlier, and her mother thought it was because he worked in the morning.

She didn't start the wipers. An hour ago she'd been sitting in his airplane looking south at his ridge, same lid on it, same snow coming. And she'd turned around at the tie down. Which, it turned out, was the cheap place to do it.

She sat there furious with him, the snow filling in the glass, and for once she let herself have it. He'd called their mother from a parking lot and told her it was a beautiful night. He got lucky on that hill and kept flying it every December, just earlier, like the clock was the problem, and then he died on a Saturday morning of the one thing nobody could have turned around for.
Her mother wasn't getting the page. Don't tell Mom. Okay, Danny. Fine. She could do that one.
She called to say she was leaving instead. 5:20 on the dash clock. First ring.
I'm driving, Ma. I'm leaving now. I'll be late.
A long silence. Then: Okay. Go slow on the hill. They're saying it's bad on the hill.

Her mother was right about the hill. Past Castle Rock the snow came straight into the headlights, every semi had its flashers going, and somewhere ahead a plow kept throwing orange light across the median. Thirty five, both hands, radio off, a Subaru riding her bumper for six miles until it gave up. Once, near the top, she looked up at the ridge and the gray sitting on it and thought about a Skylane at 8,500 under that. Then road again.

Twenty after seven when she got to Velarde's. Somebody had propped the back room door open with a chair and it was still about ninety degrees in there. Green chile, an aunt's perfume, a space heater nobody could find the switch for. Balloons on the last chair, one already sagging. Ellie's sign was by the door, one corner already curling off the tape. Airplane, backward 4. Below it, added this afternoon in a purple from some other marker, a car with wings.

Her mother had the head of the table and the good maroon cardigan, sixty three as of this morning, and hadn't touched her enchiladas. The phone lay face up by the bread basket. Eleven years of waiters had known to leave it there.

For a while her mother just looked at her. A cousin at the far end quit talking mid-story. Jordan was still in the doorway, dripping, holding the cake box out with both hands like a delivery she needed signed for.

Her mother flipped the phone. Screen down on the tablecloth, next to the bread. Half the table missed it, and the half that saw it mostly thought she was being polite. Who called? somebody's uncle wanted to know. Claire had a hand pressed flat over her mouth.

Eleven years I've sat at this table waiting for one of my kids to come down out of the sky, her mother said, to nobody in particular, to all of them. This is the first time one of my kids ever turned around.

Jordan didn't say anything. Her coat was dripping on the floor. She got the cake down a second before Ellie hit her in the knees, already mid-question. Did the car part work. Was it upslope, because Mom said upslope on the phone like twice. Was Biscuit scared. Yes, yes, and no, she's tied down, and on a night like this that's about the best a plane can hope for. Ellie took that in and asked when the flan was coming.

Flan, finally. Ellie got the burnt part, which had been negotiated in the car. Candles, then the song, English first, and on the Spanish verse the waiters came in so loud a busboy dropped a fork. Somewhere in there her mother reached over and took Jordan's hand on the tablecloth. She kept it through the coffee, eating left handed to do it. Nobody mentioned it.
At 10:52 PM, in her aunt's spare room, with an alarm set for 4:30 so she could follow the plows home and make the station by seven, her phone buzzed.

A text from Abby Strand. Rebooked. Wednesday the 16th, Pueblo, night cross-country, clear and cold all day. Your mother can have a second birthday. Then the long solo, then the written. Book the test for January. You're ready for it. You were ready for tonight too, which is the part that matters.
